concepts.decision: Apply rules to the actual data flow/threat model; document risk-owned exceptions with compensating controls, expiry, and retest.
concepts.definition: Language- and architecture-aware practices and standards that make safe implementation, review, testing, exceptions, and learning repeatable.
concepts.failureExample: A developer bypassing a rule for one deadline can create a durable cross-tenant access flaw.
concepts.label: Secure Coding

concepts.decision: Allowlist expected values and validate both syntactic and contextual/semantic rules before processing or storage.
concepts.definition: Server-side checking that received data conforms to expected syntax, type, length, range, encoding, and business semantics.
concepts.failureExample: A request with a numeric amount can still be invalid if it exceeds an authorized transfer limit.
concepts.label: Input Validation

concepts.decision: Use correct context encoding at the output sink and safe rendering APIs; preserve raw data only where needed for later safe use.
concepts.definition: Context-aware transformation of untrusted data before it is emitted to an interpreter such as HTML, attribute, URL, JavaScript, or template.
concepts.failureExample: Rendering stored notes without encoding can execute attacker-supplied markup for an administrator.
concepts.label: Output Encoding

concepts.decision: Use parameterized/bound interfaces and safe APIs, validate input, minimize interpreter use, and test malicious syntax in affected contexts.
concepts.definition: A weakness where untrusted input is interpreted as command/query/template/code structure instead of treated solely as data.
concepts.failureExample: String-concatenating an invoice ID into a query lets data alter query logic.
concepts.label: Injection

concepts.decision: Model/test abuse cases for each endpoint and protect sensitive operations with server-side checks and observability.
concepts.definition: Controls that keep programmatic interfaces safe across caller identity, object/action authority, data validation, replay/rate limits, response exposure, error behavior, and logging.
concepts.failureExample: An API that authenticates a caller but returns any requested invoice ID permits cross-tenant disclosure.
concepts.label: API Security

concepts.decision: Protect credential/token issuance, validation, expiration, revocation, and storage; require stronger assurance for higher-risk use.
concepts.definition: Proof that a user, device, or service presents valid identity credentials.
concepts.failureExample: A stolen valid session can satisfy authentication while the attacker is still unauthorized for a particular object.
concepts.label: Authentication

concepts.decision: Enforce at every protected object/action boundary using least privilege and deny by default; test negative/cross-tenant cases.
concepts.definition: Server-side decision whether the authenticated principal may take the requested action on this resource in this context.
concepts.failureExample: Only checking role “customer” allows a customer to retrieve another customer’s invoice.
concepts.label: Authorization

concepts.decision: Use managed environment-scoped retrieval, short/appropriate scope, redaction, rotation, and incident response instead of code/config hardcoding.
concepts.definition: Sensitive access material such as keys, passwords, tokens, and connection strings that must be protected throughout creation, use, rotation, and revocation.
concepts.failureExample: A secret committed to a repository may remain in history and build caches after removal.
concepts.label: Secrets

concepts.decision: Fail closed/safely where appropriate, return generic responses to callers, protect detailed logs, and test dependency/exception paths.
concepts.definition: Controlled failure behavior that protects users and system state while providing authorized diagnostics without leaking internals or credentials.
concepts.failureExample: A database exception returned to a browser reveals schema details useful for attack.
concepts.label: Error Handling

concepts.decision: Combine parameterized data access with object/row authorization, least privilege, auditing and appropriate retention/minimization.
concepts.definition: Protection of transactional and analytical data, queries, service identities and permitted data use.
concepts.failureExample: A parameterized query is injection-safe but exposes another customer’s records because authorization was omitted.
concepts.label: Database Data Warehouse Security

concepts.decision: Validate inputs server-side, enforce authorization on protected operations, and encode output for the actual output context.
concepts.definition: The browser, service, session and data-processing contexts through which a web application accepts input and produces output.
concepts.failureExample: A stored comment becomes script because the dashboard renders it as executable markup.
concepts.label: Web Application Environment

misconceptions.claim: A framework automatically prevents all injection and authorization bugs.
misconceptions.correction: Framework defaults help, but unsafe APIs, custom logic, configuration, and object-level decisions still require review and tests.

outcome: Recognize high-impact coding and API weaknesses and select standards, design practices, and tests that prevent or detect them.

sections.body: Use allow-list validation and canonicalization appropriate to context, parameterized queries, output encoding, safe memory and resource handling, secure error behavior, strong authentication and authorization, protected secrets, safe cryptography APIs, dependency hygiene, and least privilege. APIs must validate object-level authorization, replay, rate, and data exposure—not merely authenticate callers.
keyPoints: Validation and encoding solve different problems and occur at different boundaries.
Authentication identifies a caller; authorization constrains actions and objects.
Use established libraries and standards instead of inventing cryptography.
sections.title: Prevent unsafe behavior by design

sections.body: Coding standards, threat-informed review, misuse cases, linters, SAST/DAST, dependency checks, peer review, secure design patterns, and developer training make expectations repeatable. Record exceptions and risk decisions, test fixes, and feed production incidents and logs back into standards. Standards should be language- and architecture-aware without weakening core principles.
keyPoints: Automated checks are guardrails, not complete reasoning.
Review should consider data flow, trust boundaries, authorization, and failure modes.
Security guidance must be maintained as frameworks and threats change.
sections.title: Make secure coding repeatable

sections.body: Data and analytics systems need parameterized query interfaces, least-privileged service identities, object/row access decisions, protected audit, retention/minimization, and tests for unauthorized data access. Web systems need server-side validation, context-appropriate output encoding, safe session/transport behavior, authorization on each protected object/action, and safe errors. These controls complement one another: parameterization prevents data becoming query syntax; authorization decides whether the request is permitted.
keyPoints: Do not use client-side validation as a security boundary.
Do not let a valid authentication result substitute for object-level authorization.
Test database/data-warehouse and web flows with malicious, malformed, and cross-tenant requests.
sections.title: Apply secure coding to database/data-warehouse and web environments

learningJob.plainExplanation: Validation, parameterized queries, server-side object authorization, contextual output encoding, and safe errors solve different boundary problems. Applying one control at the wrong interpreter or policy boundary leaves the other weakness intact.
learningJob.visualReasoningGain: The authored boundary walkthrough keeps SQL structure, object policy, browser interpretation, and error handling distinct, enabling the learner to choose the control at the right boundary.
